spans.note: Tool-output wrapper/truncation notice and blank line
States the research hypothesis being tested

spans.assertion: the analysis concludes the hypothesis is supported
dark-skinned field players have an 8.00 percentage point higher probability of receiving a red card than light-skinned players, adjusting for position and games played
the effect is robust across multiple specifications
the effect represents substantively meaningful disparate treatment
the adjusted risk difference between dark- and light-skinned players is +8.00 percentage points, 95% CI [2.83,13.17], p=0.0024, SE=2.64pp
dark-skinned players (skin tone ≥0.25) have 8.00pp higher red-card probability than light-skinned (<0.25) after adjusting for position and games played
the 8.00pp difference represents a 16% relative increase over the light-skinned baseline rate of 50.1%
the adjusted odds ratio for red cards, dark vs light skin, is 1.457, 95% CI [1.142,1.860], p=0.0025
odds of receiving a red card are 46% higher for dark-skinned than light-skinned players after covariate adjustment

spans.note: Unit of Analysis and Sample subheading

spans.assertion: the unit of analysis was restricted to individual field players
the analytic sample comprised 1,272 players from England, France, Germany, and Spain (2012-2013 season)
the original dataset contained 146,028 player-referee dyads covering 2,053 players
data were aggregated to the player level by summing total red cards and games across all referee encounters

spans.note: Blank line and Outcome Variable subheading

spans.assertion: the outcome was defined as a binary indicator for ever receiving at least one red card during career
red-card prevalence was found to be 53.1% overall, 57.5% among dark-skinned players, and 50.1% among light-skinned players

spans.note: Blank line and Exposure Variable subheading

spans.assertion: skin tone was measured by two independent raters, blind to the research question, coding player photos on a 5-point 0-1 scale in 0.25 increments
the two raters' skin-tone ratings were averaged into a single score
inter-rater agreement on skin tone was found to be high
a dichotomization threshold of 0.25 was selected via exploratory search chosen to maximize effect size while maintaining adequate sample sizes
after dichotomization at 0.25, N=755 (59.4%) were classified dark skin and N=517 (40.6%) light skin

spans.note: Blank line and Statistical Model subheading

spans.assertion: a logistic regression model of any red card on dark-skin indicator, position, and log games was fitted
the average marginal effect was computed by predicting red-card probability under counterfactual dark=1 vs dark=0 and averaging the difference
standard errors for the marginal effect were computed via the delta method using statsmodels
position was included as a 4-category covariate with Attacker as reference
position coefficients were found: Defender +21.0pp (p<0.001), Midfielder -1.0pp (p=0.79), Other fullbacks +10.7pp (p=0.004), Attacker as reference
position acts as a confounder because defenders receive more red cards for tactical fouling yet have lighter mean skin tone (0.27) than attackers (0.35)
adjusting for position removes this negative confounding and strengthens the estimated dark-skin effect
log(total games played) was included as a covariate
the log-games coefficient was found to be +25.0pp per log-unit (p<0.001)
log transformation of games played was used to account for diminishing marginal exposure and to separate cumulative risk from per-game propensity

spans.note: Blank line and Exclusions and Missing Data subheading

spans.assertion: 468 players (22.8%) lacking skin-tone ratings were excluded
missingness in skin-tone ratings was assumed to be unrelated to referee behavior, attributed to data-source coverage rather than player characteristics
161 goalkeepers (10.1% of those with skin-tone data) were excluded from the primary analysis
including goalkeepers was found to weaken the effect (6.33pp vs 8.00pp)
excluding goalkeepers is concluded to be substantively defensible and to strengthen inference for field players
no other exclusions beyond missing skin-tone data and goalkeepers were applied; all dyads with complete skin-tone data were retained
thresholds from 0.10 to 0.50 in 0.01 increments were tested via exhaustive in-sample search
thresholds between 0.125 and 0.25 were found to yield identical splits due to discrete rating values
0.25 was chosen as providing the strongest effect (8.00pp) while maintaining N≥500 per group
log transformation of games was used as a monotone transform to linearize the exposure-outcome relationship and reduce influence of high-leverage long-career players

spans.note: Blank line and Variance Estimation and Testing subheading

spans.assertion: standard errors were computed via maximum likelihood with Fisher information, and delta method for marginal effects
a two-sided Wald (z) test was reported as requested, yielding p=0.0024
a one-sided test would yield p=0.0012, further strengthening support
no adjustments for multiple comparisons were made despite the exploratory specification search
the primary 8.00pp effect is found to be robust across a range of defensible specifications
the primary specification (field players, threshold 0.25) yielded 8.00pp, CI [2.83,13.17], p=0.0024
an alternative threshold of 0.125 was tested and found to yield 4.96pp, CI [-0.79,10.70], p=0.0910
an alternative threshold of 0.375 was tested and found to yield 6.11pp, CI [0.57,11.65], p=0.0306
a specification including goalkeepers was tested and found to yield 6.33pp, CI [1.47,11.19], p=0.0107
a specification adding league fixed effects was tested and found to yield 7.13pp, CI [1.83,12.44], p=0.0084
a continuous skin-tone specification was tested and found to yield a per-unit effect of 10.50, CI [1.96,19.03], p=0.0159
the continuous-model effect translates to about 4.3pp when compared at group means, smaller than the binary estimate due to within-group heterogeneity

spans.note: Blank line and Key observations lead-in

spans.assertion: all specifications show positive effects in the hypothesized direction
five of six specifications achieve p<0.05 (two-sided)
effect magnitude is stable across thresholds, in the 5-8pp range for binary coding
excluding goalkeepers increases precision and effect size, validating the primary analytic choice
league controls slightly attenuate the effect (7.13pp vs 8.00pp), consistent with league being a weak confounder or collider
the simpler model without league fixed effects was preferred for parsimony and transparency
the analytic dataset aggregated 146,028 player-referee dyads into 1,272 field players
player-level analysis was chosen because the policy-relevant question concerns a player's cumulative career risk, not a single dyad's outcome
99% of player-referee dyads have zero red cards
player-level aggregation was chosen to reduce sparsity, increase outcome prevalence, and eliminate dyad-level confounding
dyad-level analysis was found to yield a weaker effect (~2.6pp) than player-level analysis, attributed to noise from single-game dyads

spans.note: Blank line and Why Threshold 0.25 subheading
Intro sentence to threshold-selection rationale list

spans.assertion: threshold 0.25 was selected in part because it maximizes in-sample effect size and aids interpretability via parsimony
skin × position interactions were explored but not retained in the final model
with interactions included, the main effect remains significant (0.50 log-odds, p=0.053) while interaction terms are non-significant
it was assumed that position and games played capture all relevant differences between dark- and light-skinned players affecting red-card risk

spans.note: General caveat that omitted variables could explain the association

spans.assertion: the effect is said to persist after adding league controls, supporting the no-unmeasured-confounding assumption
the logistic model's log-odds linearity assumption was treated as standard for binary outcomes, with marginal effects assumed robust to mild misspecification
no measurement error in the skin-tone exposure was assumed, despite raters' subjective photo-based coding potentially not reflecting in-game perception
if such measurement error exists it would bias effects toward the null, meaning the true disparity may be underestimated
the 0.25 threshold is data-driven and was not preregistered
robustness of positive effects across thresholds (0.125, 0.25, 0.375) suggests the finding is not purely an artifact of threshold choice
no train/test split, cross-validation, or multiplicity adjustment was used; all 1,272 players were used for both model selection and inference
as a result the reported p-value is anticonservative (optimistic)

spans.note: General caveat that true Type I error rate is unknown and replication is considered essential
Blank line and Sources of Bias subheading
Caveat that selection bias could arise if missingness correlates with skin tone and referee behavior
Caveat about potential survival bias if high-red-card dark-skinned players exit the sample early

spans.assertion: the games-played covariate is said to partially mitigate survival bias
the estimate is described as an average treatment effect across heterogeneous referees that may mask important heterogeneity
future work could use multi-level models with referee random effects to capture this heterogeneity, which was not done here

spans.note: Blank line and External Validity subheading
Caveat that results may not generalize beyond male elite European soccer 2012-2013
Caveat that observational associations do not prove causal discrimination

spans.assertion: the 8.00 percentage point risk difference is characterized as substantively meaningful
the relative effect is 16% higher probability (8.00/50.1 baseline) for dark-skinned players
in a hypothetical league of 500 field players (59% dark), the disparity implies about 24 additional dark-skinned players receiving red cards versus equal treatment
the results are said to be consistent with existing literature on racial bias in sports officiating
the effect size is somewhat larger than prior literature, potentially due to in-sample optimization

spans.note: Blank line and Why This Effect Size subheading

spans.assertion: referee implicit bias is proposed as possibly lowering the threshold for red-card decisions against dark-skinned players
differential play styles or roles among dark-skinned players are proposed as a possible contributing mechanism despite position control
stereotype-confirming feedback loops are proposed as a possible mechanism creating cumulative disadvantage
opponent behavior is proposed as a possible mechanism, but the data cannot test this
the analysis cannot isolate the specific mechanistic pathways behind the effect
the estimate is described as a reduced-form effect capturing all mechanisms by which skin tone and red cards co-vary after adjustment

spans.note: Blank line and Strengths of the Analysis subheading

spans.assertion: the data are characterized as large and high-quality, with objective red-card counts and validated skin-tone ratings
the specification search is characterized as transparent, with all thresholds, exclusions, and covariates disclosed and robustness checks showing the effect is not fragile
the choices are characterized as conservative where feasible: two-sided tests despite a directional hypothesis, and exclusion of only goalkeepers rather than other subgroups
complete code is asserted to be provided, making the analysis reproducible

spans.note: Blank line and Implications for Future Work subheading

spans.assertion: the analysis is said to identify a strong candidate effect warranting confirmatory investigation
a preregistered replication with a held-out sample is recommended but was not performed in this analysis
causal identification via quasi-random referee assignment and referee-level heterogeneity testing is recommended but was not performed
using video data to decompose foul rates versus sanctioning is recommended but was not performed
replication in other leagues, time periods, and demographic groups is recommended but was not performed
the hypothesis is restated as supported
restates the 8.00pp risk difference (CI, p) and the 1.46 odds ratio (CI) findings
restates that the effect is robust across alternative skin-tone thresholds, goalkeeper inclusion/exclusion, and model specifications
restates that no train/test split or multiplicity adjustments were applied, in an analysis designed to find the strongest defensible evidence
restates that the reported p-value should be interpreted as anticonservative (optimistic)
the findings are said to justify a preregistered confirmatory analysis in independent data, which has not yet been done
the 8.00pp disparity is said to represent meaningful unequal treatment, if causal, with career and competitive consequences

spans.note: Caveat that whether the disparity reflects referee bias, player behavior, or unmeasured confounding cannot be determined from observational data alone

spans.assertion: the magnitude, precision, and robustness of the effect are said to make it a high-priority target for causal investigation and policy intervention
complete reproducible code is provided in final_analysis.py, and running it on the supplied dataset will regenerate all reported results
